sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

Case F53: segment the fibrous soft-tissue tumor on this T2-weighted MRI.

Volume: 381x381x69 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

content.thinking: I'll start by opening the case to begin working through it.

content.text:
case F53 | sequence T2 | shape (i,j,k)=(381, 381, 69) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: fibrous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).

I'm wondering if this is the fibrous tumor itself showing cystic or myxoid change, though fibrous lesions are usually darker on T2, so the brightness might just be unsuppressed fat rather than tumor tissue.

The dark-gray posterior structure with fine bright vessel-like lines could be the popliteal vessels running through muscle. content.thinking:
Looking at axial slice 19 with the full view, I'm trying to parse the limb cross-section anatomy — the bright lobulated structure anteriorly with dark septations could be bone or fat, while the dark-gray homogeneous oval posteriorly with bright vessel lines looks like it could be the calf muscle.

I'm checking the scale bar to estimate real measurements and figure out whether the anterior bright structure is consistent with bone marrow or something else — but the size calculation seems too large for a tibia, so I'm reconsidering the identification.

Recalculating the body width suggests a cross-section closer to a thigh or hip, roughly 250 mm across, which seems large unless this is a bigger patient or there's a mass present. I'm weighing whether the anterior bright lobulated region could be the femur's marrow cavity, but at ~115 mm it's far too big for that, so I'm now wondering if it represents a large lesion instead.

Tracking the bright structure through the slice series, it appears across roughly 35 slices and spans about 100×80 mm in-plane, which points toward a sizeable mass rather than normal anatomy. The posterior dark oval region, by contrast, spans a much broader slice range and looks more consistent with a large muscle group bounded by fascia, with faint bright streaks that could be intramuscular fat.

I'm second-guessing which structure actually represents the tumor. Fibrous soft-tissue tumors like desmoids are usually dark to intermediate on T2 and fairly homogeneous, which better matches the posterior gray mass rather than the bright anterior one — even though fibrosarcoma-type lesions with hemorrhage or necrosis could appear heterogeneous and bright instead.

I need to compare the signal of the bright anterior structure against the subcutaneous fat rim to see if it's actually fat-containing, which would point toward something like lipofibromatosis rather than a pure fibrous tumor.

Checking the scale bar against the overall body cross-section width, it seems the FOV corresponds to roughly 2 display pixels per mm, meaning this cross-section measures around 250 mm wide—quite large, so I'm reconsidering whether this is really a knee-level slice or a larger thigh/hip region.

I'm puzzling over that bright ring structure near the anterior-right side—it could be a vessel like the great saphenous vein or femoral vessel showing some flow pattern, but I'm not fully certain yet. I think I need to look at adjacent axial slices to get better context on the posterior dark structure and confirm what anatomy is actually present.

Trying to pin down whether this is the knee or lower leg region, the anterior bright lobulated structure with a thin dark cortex-like rim could be bone marrow with trabecular pattern, suggesting the tibial plateau or distal femur, while the posterior dark homogeneous oval might be a fibrous tumor mass or calf musculature. The laterality is confusing me—tracking patient right versus image left to figure out if this is tibia versus fibula placement isn't adding up cleanly, and the size (~110mm) seems too large for a tibia alone, so I'm considering whether it's actually a fatty mass like a lipoma rather than normal bone marrow. I think the best path forward is pulling up more full-view slices, particularly around axial 0 and axial 45, to clarify the anatomy before committing to an interpretation.

content.thinking:
At slice 46 the signal looks very dark, which could mean coil sensitivity drops off at superior levels, or this is a different anatomical region entirely. I'm seeing a dark anterior region and posterior muscle group, with that large oval posterior shape being consistent with muscle tissue—this intensity falloff pattern suggests the coil's field strength is highest inferiorly, explaining why slices 0-30 appear brighter.

But comparing the anterior bright structure against the posterior dark region more carefully, they look like genuinely different tissue types—heterogeneous bright anteriorly versus medium gray with bright vessel lines posteriorly. Given the 69-slice, 1mm coverage, this seems like a limited-coverage T2 sequence over a small region, and I'm now thinking the "tumor" is likely the anterior bright lobulated mass spanning slices 0-35, though its broad flat shape (35mm superior-inferior, 100mm in-plane) would fit with an infiltrative fibrous tumor.

Looking more closely at slice 6, I'm trying to place this anatomically at the knee level—patella anteriorly, femoral condyles, popliteal vessels posteriorly, calf muscles. The lobulated bright structure with dark septations could actually be a joint effusion or synovial process like a Baker's cyst or pigmented villonodular synovitis rather than a classic fibrous tumor.

This matches the pattern of tenosynovial giant cell tumor/PVNS, which falls under the fibrohistiocytic tumor category alongside desmoid fibromatosis and nodular fasciitis. The lobulated, heterogeneous appearance with dark hemosiderin-related blooming spots amid brighter fluid signal is a classic MRI signature for PVNS, which fits well with the structure I'm seeing at the knee joint.

I'm also second-guessing the scale here—the cross-sectional width of roughly 250 mm seems too wide for a typical knee at the joint line, which usually measures closer to 100 mm across. This makes me wonder if I'm actually looking at a thigh level closer to the hip, or if this is simply a larger-bodied individual, since the metadata does indicate 1mm isotropic spacing that I should trust.

Working through the slice coverage, I'm trying to pin down whether the bright anterior structure in the inferior slices is the proximal tibia or a distinct soft tissue mass—the fact that it's bounded on both the inferior and superior ends in the stack argues against it being bone, since bone would typically continue toward the joint rather than terminating abruptly. I'm cataloging three candidate structures: the bright heterogeneous anterior mass in the lower slices, the dark homogeneous posterior oval, and a smaller anterior-left blob appearing in the upper slices, and trying to cross-reference their positions between the coronal and sagittal views to figure out how they spatially relate.

Given this is likely a sarcoma-type dataset with a labeled fibrous soft-tissue tumor, I'm leaning toward the lobulated anterior mass with internal septations as the most likely candidate for the lesion, but I want to verify its shape and extent by viewing a full-crop sagittal slice through its center along with a corresponding coronal slice.

content.text: axial 12/69 | crop full | marks coarse | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 10/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:
At axial slice 12, this anterior bright structure appears large and lobulated, with a bright rim and a dark-speckled interior that's more homogeneous and gray on the patient's right, while the left side shows a honeycomb texture. It's bounded by a dark fascial or capsular rim, with a gray region anterior to it near the far left of the image.

Posteriorly, I notice a large dark-gray zone containing a bright branching tubular structure, likely representing vessels with flow-related signal—possibly popliteal vein/artery branches—suggesting this region corresponds to the popliteal fossa or posterior compartment. The surrounding dark-gray tissue is probably muscle (gastrocnemius/semimembranosus) rather than fat, since the subcutaneous fat at the periphery appears comparatively bright, which would mean fat isn't suppressed here and the posterior darkness is muscle rather than fat-saturated tissue.

I'm trying to locate bone, but nothing in this slice clearly resembles cortex. The anterior bright structure with a dark rim and honeycomb-like interior could represent trabecular bone with marrow, but checking against patella dimensions—roughly 40-50mm wide, 30mm AP—our structure at 115mm wide doesn't match unless the scale bar itself is miscalibrated.

Scaling up to a large thigh doesn't fit either, since even a large femur would only be ~35-50mm in diameter, far smaller than the 115 × 85mm anterior structure—so this must be a mass rather than normal bone. I'm now wondering if this lobulated, heterogeneous anterior mass with its bright rim and honeycomb pattern could be a fibrous or myxoid tumor, while the posterior dark region with vessels represents normal muscle or the popliteal area—or alternatively, the posterior oval could be the actual tumor target and the anterior structure just normal fat-containing tissue like Hoffa's fat pad.

The distinct borders and marked heterogeneity make me lean toward the anterior structure being the actual tumor rather than a normal structure. I'm also considering whether this "popcorn-like" pattern of bright rim and dark spots could represent PVNS (pigmented villonodular synovitis) in the suprapatellar pouch, though that would typically be bounded by the femur and tibia within the joint capsule, which doesn't quite match what I'm seeing here with the separating dark band.

Since the mass vanishes above slice 37 while PVNS would typically span multiple slices across the joint, I'm leaning back toward this being a fibrous soft-tissue tumor case where the anterior honeycomb mass is the primary lesion, with the posterior dark oval likely representing normal muscle like the gastrocnemius or hamstrings. I'm also wondering if the small anterior-left blob seen in slices 37-56 is just the same mass tapering as it extends superiorly.

Looking across several axial slices, I'm tracking faint gray structures and a notably bright blob at slice 56 that could be a vessel, fluid pocket, or the mass's superior tail. I think the best approach now is to use a seg_point click on the anterior mass at a slice where it's largest, like axial 12 or 19, then verify its 3D extent across the sheets, keeping in mind nnInteractive might leak segmentation into surrounding tissue. I'm now picking out candidate interior points within the honeycomb mass at slice 12 to use as the click location.

Given how heterogeneous this mass looks, I'm leaning toward a box or lasso prompt instead of a single point, since nnInteractive handles irregular lesions better that way. I'm scanning the available marks around the mass's boundary to assemble a rough bounding box or polygon outline, though the marks are sparse and not perfectly positioned at the corners, so I'll need to pick the closest ones and accept some imprecision.

Before committing to segmentation, I want to double check the mass's plausible size (roughly 100x80mm in-plane, consistent with a sarcoma) and also verify whether it connects to those fainter structures seen in slices 37–56. To refine my point selection, I'll call seg_view on axial 12 cropped to the relevant marks, and also try the edge-marks mode to get a cleaner boundary outline for a lasso prompt, trading off against my limited remaining tool calls.

I'm reconsidering whether the anterior mass could be sclerotic bone rather than soft tissue, then checking the sagittal and coronal views to see if that structure connects continuously to the tibial shaft like bone, or instead has its own capsule suggesting a soft-tissue mass. Given the task description points toward a fibrous soft-tissue tumor, I'm now looking elsewhere for a dark-T2 mass, since the posterior muscle compartment appears otherwise unremarkable, and scanning further slices for another bright or atypical focus.

I'm also cross-checking the posterior oval seen at slices 37-68, wondering if it represents femoral condyles or just muscle, and revisiting the sagittal series where the bright structure consistently sits anterior-inferior across multiple sagittal positions, suggesting it spans roughly 130mm in the x-direction with a fairly consistent superior boundary.

This rounded margin, heterogeneous internal signal, and clear rim make me lean toward a soft-tissue mass rather than tibial anatomy, since a honeycomb pattern with curvilinear low-signal septa is actually characteristic of myxoid tumors like myxofibrosarcoma or myxoid liposarcoma—where T2-bright myxoid matrix is crossed by dark fibrous strands creating that swirled, serpentine appearance.

So I'm leaning toward segmenting the anterior bright honeycomb mass as the target lesion, treating the more homogeneous left portion as a less myxoid component of the same tumor, while the posterior oval region with intermediate signal and crossing vessels looks like normal muscle rather than a second mass.

Now I need to trace the mass boundary using the lasso tool, working through the E-numbered marks in the zoomed panel to outline the outer edge including the bright rim, starting from the top-left corner and moving clockwise around the lesion.

I keep working through the rest of the E-markers one by one, noting each label's position alongside its marker coordinates and color (black or blue outline) as I map them across the right side and bottom of the panel.
